# Mission

This EDA has two subjects.

The first is the **three mutually exclusive outcome groups** we constructed to think
through the numerical nature of the outcome: No Days, Chronic Days, and Non-Chronic
Days. They are exhaustive, they partition the analytic sample, and they will be the
frame in which model results and group comparisons are read.

The second is the **distribution of `days_absent`**, the numeric outcome, and what
happens to it under coarsening. Chronic days are not a separate measure; they are the
portion of `days_absent` attributed to a chronic condition. Graphs that show the
whole measure and graphs that show the chronic component are labelled and coloured
differently so the two are never conflated.

Graph family g2 is then offered as an **illustration**: one way a set of variables --
here the project's predisposing domain -- can be evaluated against those three groups.
The substance is the method, not the predisposing findings. Family g3 is a reference
profile of the No Days group, kept for lookup.

**Research Questions:**

1.  How do the three outcome groups partition the analytic sample, and how are they
    defined from the two day counts?
2.  How is `days_absent_total` distributed among respondents who missed any work, and
    how do the exact, five-day, and hybrid scales change what a reader sees?
3.  How does the chronic component sit inside that measure, in support and in shape?
4.  How do the two positive-day groups compare when both are placed on the same
    measure?
5.  How can a set of candidate variables be evaluated against the three groups, using
    the predisposing domain as the worked example?

# Definition of Terms

**`days_absent_total`** ("days absent"): workdays missed for any health reason in the
past three months. Support 0-63. This is the numeric outcome.

**`days_absent_chronic`** ("chronic days"): the portion of those same days attributed
to a chronic condition. Support 0-31. It is a **component of** `days_absent_total`,
not a parallel measure. Every respondent satisfies
`days_absent_chronic <= days_absent_total`.

**No Days**: `days_absent_total == 0` (n = 45,006).

**Chronic Days**: `days_absent_chronic > 0` (n = 3,626). This group may also report
non-chronic absence days.

**Non-Chronic Days**: `days_absent_chronic == 0 & days_absent_total > 0`
(n = 15,211).

**Work-week coarsening**: Five reported workdays are grouped into one display week.
This is a scale-design choice, not a claim about elapsed time or work schedule.

**Colour convention**: The outcome-group palette is grey (No Days), reddish brown
(Chronic Days), and dark blue (Non-Chronic Days). Every sequential ramp in this report
inherits from it. A **bluish** ramp means the display is of `days_absent_total`, the
whole measure. A **reddish** ramp means the display is of the chronic component.

# Analysis

## Graph Family g1: Outcome Groups and the Days-Absent Scale

This family carries both subjects of the report. The **outcome-group partition** --
No Days, Chronic Days, Non-Chronic Days -- is reproduced unchanged at the left of
every graph below, so that each view of the numeric outcome is read against the
population it comes from. The panels at right show `days_absent_total` at the exact
scale and at two coarsenings.

The exact support of `days_absent_total` runs from 1 to 63 among respondents who
missed any work. The chronic component runs only from 1 to 31. That difference is not
a rounding artifact; it follows from chronic days being one of eight reasons summed
into the total.

```{r}

#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| cache: true
```

```

### g11 - Days Absent at Three Scales

Graph g11 places the three-way cohort partition at left and, at right, the
distribution of `days_absent_total` among all 18,837 respondents who missed at least
one day -- the Chronic and Non-Chronic groups combined. The three right-hand panels
hold the same people at the exact, five-day work-week, and first-week-exact scales.
The bluish ramp signals the whole measure.

Read the panels against each other: the five-day binning collapses the first five
one-day bars, which is where most of the mass sits, into a single 15,176-respondent
column. The hybrid scale is the compromise that keeps that structure visible while
still taming the tail.

```

#### g111 - The Chronic Component at the Same Three Scales

Graph g111 repeats the g11 construction on the chronic component alone. It is the
same design, the same three scales, and the same partition panel; only the measure and
the basis change. The reddish ramp signals the subset.

Two differences are worth naming. The support ends at day 31 rather than 63, and the
terminal value carries visible mass -- 251 respondents report exactly 31 chronic days,
which is consistent with a reporting ceiling rather than a smooth tail.

### g12 - Both Positive-Day Groups on the Same Measure

Graph g12 compares the two positive-day groups on one measure, `days_absent_total`.
An earlier version of this graph used chronic days for one group and total days for
the other while labelling both "missed days"; that comparison was not like-for-like
and has been withdrawn. Bar colour is the group colour from the partition panel.

Within each row, the first panel preserves days 1 through 5 and the second groups the
remaining tail into work-week bins 2 through 13. Row scales are free, so the two rows
show shape rather than magnitude; the left panel carries the magnitude.

#### g121 - Two Measures on the Same Respondents

Graph g121 makes the subset relation visible on a single set of people. The 3,626
Chronic Days respondents are counted twice: once by all days absent, once by the
chronic component of those same days. The chronic row cannot extend past work-week 7,
because 31 is the component's ceiling, while the total row reaches work-week 13.

This is the graph to consult whenever a reader is tempted to treat "chronic days" and
"days absent" as interchangeable labels for the same quantity.

## Graph Family g2: Evaluating a Variable Set Against the Outcome Groups

This family is an **illustration of a method**, not a set of substantive findings.
Family g1 established the groups and the scale; this family shows one way a set of
candidate variables can be examined against those groups. The predisposing domain
serves as the worked example because it is the first block of the project's candidate
registry. The same displays would serve any other domain unchanged.

Graphs g2, g20, g21, g211, and g212 are composition contrasts and use the pooled
survey weight. Graphs g22 through g24 condition on the 3,626 Chronic Days respondents
and report the chronic component, `days_absent_chronic`, which is labelled as such.

# Appendix

Student status is excluded because the source field is suppressed and all-missing in
the PUMF. The three outcome groups are exhaustive and mutually exclusive; the g2
family shows their complete composition comparison matrix.

Retired artifact IDs: `g0` and `g01` became `g3` and `g31` when the reference profile
moved from first position to last. Per the project's artifact rules the retired IDs are
not reused.
